title: The house-builder
hook: craving named and seen; the rafters broken, the ridgepole shattered (Dhammapada 153–154)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Buddha: the one who woke up, at dawn, as the morning star rose. Your line was awake. Did you watch the light change? Day fifty-six, the last day of the night under the tree.

You know that feeling when you finally catch yourself in a pattern. The same argument, for the tenth time. The same late-night snack. The same reason for not calling someone back. And one day, instead of just doing it again, you see it. Oh. There it is. That's the thing that keeps building this. Once you've seen it, it's never quite as strong again. Tradition says that when the Buddha woke, the first words he spoke were a short poem. Not a sermon. Not a rule. A poem addressed to someone. He'd been looking for this someone for a very long time, and finally, he'd found him. Today, the house-builder.
screen: `CATCHING YOURSELF IN A PATTERN.` → `OH. THERE IT IS.` → `A POEM TO SOMEONE.`

segments.voice: The poem is in the Dhammapada, verses one fifty-three and one fifty-four, and it pictures life after life as a house being built again and again. Somebody keeps building it. For countless lives, the Buddha says, I ran on, looking for the builder of this house, and birth after birth was painful. And then, in Max Müller's translation from 1881, he speaks directly to the builder: "maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again." Tabernacle is Müller's old word for the house, a dwelling, a tent. And then the line the outline takes its image from: "All thy rafters are broken, thy ridge-pole is sundered." So who is the house-builder? The Buddhist commentaries answer: craving. Tanha, the thirst we met back on day six, the wanting that keeps building a self and a life around it, over and over. The rafters, they say, are the other stains of the mind. The ridgepole, the beam at the very top that holds the whole roof up, is ignorance. And the trick is in the verb. The builder isn't destroyed by force. He's seen. Once craving is seen clearly, it can't build in the dark anymore. That's this whole week in one poem: a seat of grass, a vow to stay, Mara's army, the earth as witness, three watches, and dawn. And at the end, one quiet sentence to the one who'd been building the whole time. House-builder, you are seen.
screen: `A HOUSE BUILT AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `THOU HAST BEEN SEEN.` · `THE BUILDER IS CRAVING.` · `SEEN, NOT FOUGHT.` · then, large: `HOUSE-BUILDER, YOU ARE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of one habit you've already seen through, even a little. Something you used to do without noticing, and now you notice. Hitting snooze. Interrupting. Checking the fridge when bored. Picture it as a small builder, busy with hammer and nails. Now, silently, speak to it the way the poem does. I see you. Not angrily. Just clearly. Notice how seeing takes some of the power out of it. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The house-builder. Craving, which builds life after life, seen at last by the Buddha: its rafters broken, its ridgepole shattered.
Your line: house-builder, you are seen. Today, when an old habit starts building, name it quietly: I see you. Day fifty-six.

howItsDone: Many Buddhists memorize and chant Dhammapada 153–154, which Theravada tradition holds were the Buddha's first words after awakening, and teachers use the house-builder to explain craving as the source of rebirth.

original.note: Pali: house-builder (gaha, house + kāraka, maker), the name for craving in Dhammapada 153–154.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poem about a broken house.
what it means: the Buddha speaks to craving, the builder of life after life, and says: I see you. you won't build again.
what a scholar hears: gahakāraka in Dhammapada 153–154; the commentary glosses the rafters (phasuka) as defilements and the ridgepole (gahakūṭa) as ignorance.

notes: Two quotations from Max Müller's Dhammapada (SBE X, 1881), verse 154. Check against the 1881 text word for word, including 'ridge-pole' hyphenation and punctuation.
Verse 153 is paraphrased ('looking for the builder... birth after birth was painful').
First words after awakening: the Dhammapada commentary and Theravada tradition; the Vinaya gives the Udana verses instead. The script says 'tradition says'. Confirm.
Commentarial glosses (rafters = defilements, ridgepole = ignorance): confirm.
